# Market landscape — evidence-to-requirements & product decision tools

_Researched 2026-10-12 (web search). Purpose: who else works in this space if SharkSight is generalized beyond BMW into a tool anyone can use for ground-up requirements engineering and product decisions. Most sources are vendor pages or vendor-written comparisons, so funding, customer and feature claims are **company-reported** unless noted. Features not checked are marked as such._

## TL;DR

- **Nobody covers the whole chain end to end.** SharkSight's chain is: raw evidence (feedback, studies, sales, web) → findings → measurable requirements → fit/feasibility gates → explainable per-segment priority → human decision → append-only audit, re-run over time. The market splits into tools that stop at **"themes / opportunities"** (feedback intelligence, PM suites) and tools that start from **requirements someone has already written** (requirements management / ALM, systems engineering).
- **Closest threat from above: Productboard Spark** (June 2026). Agents for voice of customer, competitive research, prioritization and specs. Every insight links back to a customer note, and edits are previewed before they are saved. Its ranking logic is not explained, and the launch post mentions no audit trail.
- **Closest threat from below: Flow Engineering.** An AI-native "systems graph" for hardware teams; Rivian uses it for all R1/R2 requirements. It raised a $50M Series B at a $750M valuation on 2026-10-02. Flow starts at engineering requirements, not at customer evidence.
- **Consolidation is fast.** Amplitude bought Kraftful (Jul 2025), Atlassian bought Cycle (Sep 2025) for Jira Product Discovery, and Altium bought Valispace (2023/24). Feedback-to-insight is becoming a feature inside larger suites.
- **Where we could win:** traceable, auditable, segment-aware requirements for **physical / long-cycle / regulated products** (automotive, industrial, medtech, aerospace, consumer hardware). Here the decision is expensive, the PM must defend it, and the SaaS-oriented feedback tools don't fit well.

## 1. Our chain, stated generically

| Step | SharkSight today (BMW) | Generic form |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | verbatims, customer study, sales, option lists, cited web research (T1–T3) | any feedback + quantitative studies + market data + web research, with provenance |
| Findings | clusters, insights, themes, evidence graph | same |
| Requirements | customer-experienced metric + target ladder, horizon, Kano, evidence vs. assumption | same, domain-agnostic |
| Gates | brand & segment fit, platform/plant feasibility | pluggable gates (brand, feasibility, compliance, strategy) |
| Prioritization | prio-v1 per requirement × line × market, factor breakdown, bundles | per requirement × product line × segment |
| Decision | PM approves / rejects / defers with rationale; AI only proposes | same |
| Audit & continuity | append-only `audit_event`, checkpoints, change proposals | same |

## 2. Landscape by category

### A. Customer-feedback intelligence (upstream; stops at themes)

| Tool | What it does | Where it stops |
|---|---|---|
| **Enterpret** | Adaptive taxonomy over feedback from 50+ channels; launched an "agentic customer intelligence platform" Oct 2025. $20.8M Series A (Dec 2024, Canaan); customers incl. Canva, Notion, Strava. | Insights and alerts; no requirement model, no decision record |
| **Unwrap.ai** | Theme detection over many sources (claims 3,000+ connectors); pushes emerging themes to Slack/email | Same |
| **Dovetail** | Research repository → "customer intelligence platform". July 2026 launch: background agents, **customer "digital twins"** built from what segments said, MCP connectors (Claude, Copilot, Slack, Linear), ISO 42001 | Research synthesis; no prioritization or requirements |
| **Kraftful → Amplitude** | LLM analysis of tickets and app reviews, top requests and complaints; acquired Jul 2025 and folded into product analytics | Part of the analytics suite now |
| **BuildBetter** | Calls, tickets and docs → insights, 100+ integrations | Insights and docs |

### B. Product-management suites with AI (midstream; opportunity → spec)

| Tool | What it does | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Productboard Spark** (2026-06-22) | Agents for VoC synthesis, competitive research, prioritization, codebase-grounded PRDs; "every insight links back to a real customer note"; previews edits before saving; ranked opportunities (beta); specs go out via MCP to Claude Code / Codex / Cursor | **Closest overall.** Ranking method not explained; no audit trail mentioned; software-product oriented (codebase grounding) |
| **Jira Product Discovery** (+ **Cycle** acquisition, Sep 2025) | AI organizes feedback and connects it to ideas and delivery; Rovo agents; 20k+ customers | Feedback → ideas inside the Atlassian stack |
| **ChatPRD** | AI PRD writer; bootstrapped; claims 100k+ PMs | Document generation, not evidence |
| Aha!, ProdPad, airfocus, Canny, Pendo | Roadmap / idea tools adding AI on top of a user-maintained structure | AI features not checked in this pass |
| Zeda.io | Feedback → roadmap with revenue scoring | A competitor says it is shutting down in 2026 (unverified) |

### C. Classic requirements management / ALM (downstream; starts from written requirements)

| Tool | AI angle | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Jama Connect** | Advisor (NLP quality checks on wording), Trace Scores | Strong in regulated product development |
| **IBM DOORS Next**, **Siemens Polarion**, **PTC Codebeamer**, **Visure** | Quality checks, test generation, risk scoring (varies) | Incumbents in automotive and aerospace. No native Polarion AI assistant found; a community MCP server exposes Polarion items to LLMs |
| **Modern Requirements (Copilot4DevOps)** | Scores requirement quality against "6 C's", generates user stories, Gherkin and tests inside Azure DevOps | Authoring help, not elicitation from evidence |
| **Dassault CATIA R2026x** | "Generative systems requirement creation"; Virtual Companions (Feb 2026) for requirements alignment | Engineering-side, PLM-bound |

**Common gap:** these tools assume requirements already exist. AI improves wording, traceability and tests, not *which* requirements customers need.

### D. AI-native systems engineering (downstream, newer)

| Tool | Facts |
|---|---|
| **Flow Engineering** | "Systems graph" linking requirements, CAD, code, simulations, tests and certification. Agents log changes, flag downstream effects and check requirement and test coverage. Rivian runs all R1/R2 requirements on it (scaled to ~1,500 users in 7 months). Series A $23M (Sequoia, Oct 2025); Series B $50M at $750M (Valor / Atreides, 2026-10-02). |
| **Trace.Space** (Riga) | "AI-native requirements management": trace graph from PDFs, Jira, Git and Confluence; change impact, duplicate detection, standards compliance. $4M seed (Cherry Ventures, Feb 2025). |
| **Valispace** (Altium) | AI-assisted systems and requirements engineering for hardware; acquired by Altium (Dec 2023 / 2024). |

These are the natural **hand-off target** for our output (customer requirements → engineering requirements), not direct competitors.

### E. Market & competitive intelligence (the web-evidence layer)

**Crayon**, **Klue** (Gartner 2026 MQ Leaders for competitive and market intelligence) and **AlphaSense** (financial and strategic research, 500M+ documents). They feed sales and strategy teams. None turns competitive facts into requirements.

### F. Preference research & synthetic customers (the "how much do they want it" layer)

- **Qualtrics**, **Conjointly**, **Quantilope**, **OpinionX**: conjoint, MaxDiff and Kano studies; AI mostly helps with survey building and text analysis.
- **Synthetic customers:** **Simile** ($100M Series A Feb 2026, $200M Series B Aug 2026 at $2B; "agentic twins" trained on consented interviews) and **Aaru** (~$1B valuation). Plus Dovetail's digital twins. Trust is still low (one report: 8% of researchers fully trust synthetic alternatives). For us this is a possible *future-needs* input, but it should be labelled an **assumption, not evidence** (rule 4).

### G. Decision-intelligence platforms (adjacent, different job)

The first Gartner MQ for Decision Intelligence Platforms came out on 2026-01-26. Leaders per vendor releases: Quantexa, FICO, IBM; also Aera, o9, Pega, SAS and others. These platforms cover **operational, repeated decisions** (credit, supply chain, fraud), not one-off product-portfolio decisions. They are still useful vocabulary: governance, explainability, decision records.

### H. Industry services (automotive)

**J.D. Power** brings customer voice into OEM strategy and development, assigning requirements and priorities per vehicle system (consulting plus data such as AutoPlanner). **NTT Data** offers GenAI VoC agents (RAG + knowledge graphs) for automotive. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

Market scan · 12 Oct 2026 · SharkSight generalization

Who else turns customer evidence into product requirements?

A scan of about 20 tools in 9 categories, made to judge whether SharkSight could become a general tool for building requirements from evidence and making product decisions, beyond the BMW challenge.

Most sources are vendor pages or vendor-written comparisons, so funding, customer and feature figures are company-reported unless stated otherwise. Features I did not check are marked as such.

In short

  • No tool covers the whole chain. Feedback and product-management tools stop at themes or opportunities. Requirements and engineering tools start from requirements someone has already written.
  • Closest from upstream: Productboard Spark (June 2026). Agents for customer feedback, competitive research, prioritization and specs. Every insight links to a customer note, and edits are previewed before they are saved. Public material doesn't explain the ranking or mention an audit trail.
  • Closest from downstream: Flow Engineering. An AI-native engineering graph; Rivian runs all R1/R2 requirements on it. Raised $50M at a $750M valuation on 2 Oct 2026. It starts at engineering requirements, not at customer evidence.
  • The upstream market is consolidating. Amplitude bought Kraftful, Atlassian bought Cycle, Altium bought Valispace. Turning feedback into insights is becoming a feature inside larger suites.
  • Opening: traceable, auditable, segment-aware requirements for physical, long-cycle or regulated products, where decisions are expensive and have to be defended.

The chain we are comparing against

SharkSight's BMW pipeline, stated so it applies to any product line and any customer segment.

EvidenceFeedback, studies, sales, cited web research with provenance and trust tier
FindingsClusters, insights, themes, evidence graph
RequirementsMeasurable metric, target ladder, horizon, evidence vs. assumption
GatesBrand fit, feasibility; generically: pluggable checks
PriorityPer requirement × product line × segment, factor breakdown
DecisionOnly a person approves, with a rationale; AI proposes
Audit & timeAppend-only trail, snapshots, change proposals

Coverage by category

My assessment from public material, so a rough guide rather than a measurement. A half dot means the step is covered partly or only for one kind of input.

Feedback intelligence

The landscape

A. Customer-feedback intelligence

upstream · stops at themes
EnterpretAdaptive taxonomy over feedback from 50+ channels; agentic platform launched Oct 2025. $20.8M Series A (Dec 2024, Canaan); customers incl. Canva, Notion, Strava.Insights and alerts; no requirement model or decision record
Unwrap.aiTheme detection across many sources (claims 3,000+ connectors); pushes emerging themes to Slack and email.Same
DovetailResearch repository turned "customer intelligence platform". July 2026: background agents, customer digital twins built from what segments said, MCP connectors, ISO 42001.Research synthesis; no prioritization
Kraftful → AmplitudeLLM analysis of tickets and app reviews; acquired Jul 2025 and folded into product analytics.Now part of an analytics suite
BuildBetterCalls, tickets and docs into insights; 100+ integrations.Insights and documents

B. Product-management suites with AI

midstream · opportunity → spec
Productboard SparkAgents for customer-feedback synthesis, competitive research, prioritization and PRDs grounded in the codebase. Insights link to customer notes; edits previewed before saving; ranked opportunities (beta); specs exported to coding agents via MCP.Ranking not explained; no audit trail mentioned; built for software products
Jira Product Discovery + CycleAI connects feedback to ideas and delivery work; Rovo agents; Cycle acquired Sep 2025; 20k+ customers.Inside the Atlassian stack
ChatPRDAI PRD writer; bootstrapped; claims 100k+ PMs.Writes documents, not evidence
Aha!, ProdPad, airfocus, Canny, PendoRoadmap and idea tools adding AI on top of a structure the user maintains.AI features not checked

C. Requirements management / ALM

downstream · starts from written requirements
Jama ConnectAdvisor checks requirement wording; Trace Scores for traceability.Strong in regulated product development
DOORS Next, Polarion, Codebeamer, VisureQuality checks, test generation, risk scoring, varying by vendor. No native Polarion AI assistant found; a community MCP server exposes its work items to LLMs.Incumbents in automotive and aerospace
Modern RequirementsCopilot4DevOps scores requirement quality on "6 C's" and generates user stories, Gherkin and tests in Azure DevOps.Authoring help, not elicitation
Dassault CATIA R2026xGenerative systems-requirement creation; role-based Virtual Companions (Feb 2026).Engineering side, tied to PLM

These tools assume the requirements already exist. Their AI improves wording, traceability and tests, not the choice of which requirements customers need.

D. AI-native systems engineering

downstream · a hand-off target
Flow Engineering"Systems graph" linking requirements, CAD, code, simulations, tests and certification; agents log changes and flag downstream effects. Rivian runs all R1/R2 requirements on it (~1,500 users in 7 months). $23M Series A (Sequoia, Oct 2025); $50M Series B at $750M (2 Oct 2026).Starts at engineering requirements
Trace.SpaceRiga-based AI-native requirements management: trace graph from PDFs, Jira, Git and Confluence; change impact, duplicates, standards compliance. $4M seed (Cherry Ventures, Feb 2025).Engineering requirements
Valispace (Altium)AI-assisted systems and requirements engineering for hardware; acquired by Altium around 2023–24.Electronics toolchain

E–I. Adjacent layers

inputs, vocabulary, prior art
  • Competitive intelligence: Crayon and Klue (Leaders in Gartner's 2026 Magic Quadrant for competitive and market intelligence), AlphaSense for financial and strategic research. They serve sales and strategy teams; none turns competitor facts into requirements.
  • Preference research: Qualtrics, Conjointly, Quantilope and OpinionX run conjoint, MaxDiff and Kano studies; AI mostly helps build surveys.
  • Synthetic customers: Simile ($200M at a $2B valuation, Aug 2026) and Aaru (~$1B). Trust is still low; for us they would be an assumption input, not evidence.
  • Decision-intelligence platforms: Gartner's first Magic Quadrant (Jan 2026) lists Quantexa, FICO and IBM as Leaders. They handle repeated operational decisions (credit, fraud, supply chain), not product portfolios.
  • Automotive services: J.D. Power and NTT Data sell customer-voice-to-product-planning work as consulting, which shows OEMs currently buy this as a service.
  • Research and open source: OpenReq (EU H2020) built recommenders, group decision support for release planning and feedback analytics; it is the closest academic ancestor. A 2025 review of 74 studies on LLMs for requirements engineering found no end-to-end evidence-to-decision system. StrictDoc, Doorstop and sphinx-needs are possible export targets.

What nobody else combines

Requirements, not just insights

A measurable customer-experienced metric and a target ladder, with every number tagged cited, projected, assumption or gap.

Mixed evidence with provenance

Feedback, studies, sales and cited web research in one graph, with trust tiers and conflicts shown.

Scoring per segment

The same requirement is scored per product line × market, and cross-market conflicts are visible.

Explainable scoring

A deterministic factor breakdown the PM can re-weight, where Spark's ranking is opaque in public material.

Decision governance

AI proposes, a person decides with a rationale, every change is logged and snapshotted over time.

Pluggable gates and future needs

Brand fit and feasibility become generic checks; the 3–5-year projection stays separate from evidence.

If we generalize

  • Position as the layer between customer-feedback tools and requirements tools. Take data in from Dovetail, Enterpret, call tools, surveys and spreadsheets; hand off to Jira, Jama, Polarion, Flow, ReqIF or StrictDoc. MCP connectors are now standard (Spark, Dovetail and Crayon all ship them).
  • Start with physical, long-cycle products: automotive OEMs and suppliers, industrial equipment, medtech, consumer electronics. They rely on consultants and spreadsheets today.
  • Make it configurable: brand, model and market become organization, product line and segment. Brand-fit and plant/platform checks become a gate plug-in. The BMW file loaders become a generic import with column mapping, and the 3D car becomes an optional product visualizer with a 2D fallback.
  • Risks: Productboard or Atlassian could add audit trails and per-segment scoring, or Flow could move upstream into customer evidence. Extraction with LLMs is turning into a commodity, so the advantage has to come from the requirement model, the governance and the integrations. Enterprise buyers will expect redaction, no training on their data and certifications such as ISO 42001.

when you think that this app converted something into a generic idea not only for bmw but for all kinds of requirement engineering (maybe we also include agile form of it), what kind of name comes to your mind for the application

These are the names I'd consider. The ones I like most come first.

**My pick: Warrant**
- In argument theory (Toulmin's model), a *warrant* is what links evidence to a claim. That's exactly what the app does: customer evidence → finding → requirement, with the reasoning shown.
- It also means "to justify". Every requirement is *warranted*, and the PM signs off on it.
- It works for both a 5-year vehicle program and a 2-week sprint.
- Tagline: *"Every requirement, warranted."*
- Downside: some people will think of an arrest warrant first.

**Strong alternatives**
- **Cairn** is a stack of stones that marks a trail. Evidence is stacked into requirements, and each marker shows the way taken, which fits the audit trail and the living, re-run process. It's short, calm and easy to brand.
- **Lateral** keeps the shark identity. A shark's *lateral line* is the organ that senses faint signals in the water, here customer signals. It's a nice nod to SharkSight for anyone who gets the reference.
- **Because**: every requirement has a "because", and the app shows it. It's friendly and memorable, but hard to search for and to trademark.
- **Plumbline** is the tool that tells you what's true and level, so it fits explainable, evidence-based priorities. It sounds more engineering-oriented.

**More playful options**
- **Reqon**: requirements + reconnaissance (web research agents, scanning evidence).
- **Groundwork**: building requirements from the ground up, and it sounds agile. It's probably crowded as a brand.

**What I'd avoid**
- **Verdict, Oracle, Decide**: they suggest the AI decides, which contradicts your core rule that the PM decides.
- **Anything with "Req" or "Spec" up front**: they sound like legacy requirements tools such as DOORS or Jama, which is the category you're trying to sit above.

I haven't checked trademarks, domains, or whether existing products already use these names. If you shortlist two or three, I can run a quick availability check.

Bence işin anahtarı şu: çekirdeği metottan bağımsız tutmak, metotları da üstüne takılan **"metot paketleri"** olarak eklemek. Bugün SharkSight'ı değerli kılan şeyler aslında metottan bağımsız: izlenebilirlik, kanıtı varsayımdan ayırmak, kararı insanın vermesi, audit trail. Değişmesi gereken şeyler ise artifact tipleri, hiyerarşi, önceliklendirme modeli ve çalışma ritmi.

## 1. Çekirdek: genel zincir

Bugünkü zincir (evidence → finding → requirement → gate → priority → decision → audit) şu hale gelmeli:

**Sinyal → İçgörü → Fırsat/Problem → Çözüm/Bet → İş kalemi → Sonuç ölçümü**

Şu an eksik olan iki halka var:
- **Hipotez/varsayım nesnesi.** Bugün varsayım bir etiket. Ayrı bir nesne olursa test edilebilir, doğrulanabilir ya da çürütülebilir.
- **Sonuç ölçümü.** Lansmandan veya sprintten sonra "işe yaradı mı?" sorusu. Bu döngüyü kapatır ve gelen sonuç yeni kanıt olarak geri akar. Agile ve discovery dünyası bunsuz eksik kalır.

## 2. Metot paketleri

Her paket kendi artifact tiplerini, alanlarını, durumlarını, önceliklendirme modelini ve ritmini getirir:

| Paket | Ne ekler |
|---|---|
| **Klasik RE** (IREB, ISO 29148) | Requirement + acceptance/verification, baseline, change control, fonksiyonel olmayan gereksinimler |
| **Scrum / Agile** | Epic → feature → user story (INVEST), Gherkin acceptance criteria, Definition of Ready, story point, backlog refinement, sprint |
| **SAFe** | Portfolio epic, lean business case, WSJF, PI planning |
| **Product discovery** | Opportunity Solution Tree, Jobs-to-be-Done, hipotez → deney → öğrenme (dual-track) |
| **OKR / outcome-based** | Her gereksinimi bir objective / key result'a bağlama |
| **Lean Startup / Design Thinking** | Varsayım haritası, MVP, build–measure–learn |
| **Kanban** | Akış, WIP limiti, cycle time |
| **Stage-gate / V-model** (donanım) | Faz kapıları, doğrulama/geçerleme. Bugünkü BMW akışına en yakın paket bu. |

## 3. Önceliklendirme kütüphanesi

Bugünkü prio-v1 bu kütüphanedeki modellerden sadece biri olur. Eklenecekler: **RICE, ICE, WSJF / Cost of Delay, MoSCoW, Kano** (zaten var), **value vs. effort, AHP** ve "buy-a-feature" tarzı paydaş oylaması.

Hangi model seçilirse seçilsin bugünkü kural geçerli kalır: her skorun faktör dökümü görünür, sade dille açıklanır ve PM ağırlıkları değiştirebilir. Bu, rakiplerden ayrıştığımız noktalardan biri.

## 4. Ritim: checkpoint'ten sürekli akışa

- Checkpoint'ler (D-040) yerini **sürekli veri alımına** bırakmalı. Q-027 bunu zaten açık soru olarak tutuyor.
- Snapshot'lar sprint, PI veya çeyrek sınırına bağlanmalı. Böylece "geçen sprintten beri ne değişti?" sorusu yanıtlanabilir.
- AI'ın değişiklik önerileri, metodun kendi ritüeline (refinement, review) gelen bir öneri kutusu olarak düşmeli.

## 5. Ayrıştırma ve iki yönlü senkronizasyon

- Gereksinimden epic'e, oradan story'ye bölen bir **splitting agent**. İz hem aşağı hem yukarı korunur: bir Jira ticket'ından müşteri yorumuna kadar geri gidilebilir.
- **Jira, Linear ve Azure DevOps ile iki yönlü senkronizasyon.** Agile ekipler oradan çıkmaz, bu yüzden üstlerine konumlanmak gerekir.
- Requirements araçları için **ReqIF / OSLC**, test tarafı için **Gherkin**, AI asistanları için **MCP**.

## 6. Roller ve yönetişim

- "PM karar verir" kuralı **"karar sahibi"** olarak genelleşmeli. Scrum'da bu Product Owner, SAFe'te Epic Owner, donanımda program yöneticisi.
- Çoklu paydaş: yorum, oylama, itiraz (challenge zaten var), RACI.
- Regüle sektörler için opsiyonel bir paket: e-imza, baseline dondurma, ASPICE / ISO 26262 / FDA izlenebilirlik raporları. BMW kapsamında regülasyon dışarıdaydı, genel üründe opsiyonel olabilir.

## 7. BMW'ye özel olup config'e dönüşecekler

- Marka, model, pazar → organizasyon, ürün hattı, segment
- Brand-fit ve plant/platform kontrolü → takılıp çıkarılabilen bir **gate arayüzü** (marka, uygulanabilirlik, uyumluluk, strateji)
- BMW dosya yükleyicileri → kolon eşleştirmeli genel import
- Aspect taksonomisi → domain şablonları (SaaS, donanım, hizmet, iç IT)
- 3D araç → opsiyonel ürün görselleştirici, 2D fallback ile

## Önerdiğim sıra

1. **Çekirdek modeli genelleştir:** hipotez ve outcome nesneleri, gate arayüzü, segment ve ürün hattı config'i.
2. **Agile paketi:** story + acceptance criteria, RICE/WSJF, Jira senkronizasyonu. Pazarın en büyük kısmı burada.
3. **Discovery paketi:** Opportunity Solution Tree, deneyler, sonuç ölçümü.
4. **Regüle/donanım paketi:** bugünkü BMW akışının genelleşmiş hali.

- **Kanban neredeyse hiç önden kanıt istemez.** İhtiyacı akış verisi: cycle time, WIP, darboğaz.
- **OKR'da kanıt iki noktada önemli.** Objective seçilirken orta düzeyde kanıt gerekir. Key result ölçümü ise metodun özüdür, ama bu müşteri yorumu değil, sonuç verisidir.
- **Derin kanıt, geri alınamayan ve pahalı kararlar için gerekir:** araç ve donanım programları, platform kararları, portföy, SAFe epic'leri, regüle ürünler. BMW vakası tam olarak buydu.

**Ürüne yansıması:**
- **Üç seviyeli bir kanıt ayarı.** Hafif seviye story ve Kanban kartları için, orta seviye epic, OKR ve discovery için, derin seviye ise bugünkü SharkSight hattının tamamı.
- **Kanıt mirası.** Kanıt epic veya fırsat seviyesinde birikir, story'ler onu devralır. Böylece Jira ticket'ından müşteri yorumuna kadar iz kopmaz, ama her story için kanıt yeniden üretilmez.
- **Agile'da asıl eksik sonuç ölçümü.** Agile paketinde önden derin araştırmadan çok, sonuç ölçümünü kanıt tabanına geri bağlamak önemli. Bu yüzden önerdiğim yeni çekirdek nesnelerden biri "sonuç ölçümü".

Agile ekipleri her story'de derin kanıtla yüklemek aracın benimsenmesini öldürür. Ürünün güçlü olduğu yer sprint seviyesinin üstü: backlog'u besleyen "neden" katmanı.

Artifact özel olarak duruyor. Başkalarına göstermek istersen sayfanın Share menüsünden paylaşman gerekiyor.
